speechtext:
I should
think about the end of the present week, or the beginning of next. Some days ago the right hon. gentleman made an inquiry as to what further legislation was to be

brought down during the present session. A Bill is under consideration having for its purpose the amending of the present law respecting the liability of municipalities for the pay and subsistence of militia called out in aid of the civil power. I am not quite sure whether the measure will be ready to be brought before Parliament this session; a conclusion has been arrived at in regard to the matter, but some further consideration will be required to determine the exact nature of the proposed amendment. The Minister of Justice intends to introduce a short Bill with regard to the staffs of the penitentiaries, and I understand that it will be necessary also to amend the Judges' Act, in view of provincial legislation which has provided for an increase in the judiciary in some of the provinces. The Postmaster General expects to introduce a short Bill to amend the Post Office Act. This Bill will deal* with the salaries of letter carriers, and with some technical matters in connection with the Post Office Department. It will not, I think, be of a controversial nature. There may also be necessary amendments to the Acts establishing the departments, having regard to their organization. I am not quite sure of that, but as soon as we arrive at a conclusion I will give an intimation to my right hon. friend.

I have noticed in the
press some correspondence from business men with regard to the sending of letters to Great Britain via New York. When my hon. friend the Postmaster General laid on the table of the House the new contract for the trans-atlantic mail service, he stated that the additional number of weekly trips to Great Britain would probably do away with the sending of letters via New York. I observe that the business men in the city of Ottawa and elsewhere are complaining bitterly about this sudden change. I gathered from what the hon. gentleman said at that time that this change would take place immediately, and that, until the service was perfectly established and the new fast boats were engaged, mails could be sent by New York. Will the hon. Postmaster General explain what is being done at present?

The new service was inaugurated on the first day of the present month. I may say that no business men, nor, as a matter of fact, persons of any kind, have complained to me, although I have seen the reports in the papers to which my hon. friend refers, and I understand that some newspaper editors have telephoned the department with regard to the matter. I would like it to be distinctly
understood that we do not wish to prevent the people from sending letters via New York if they so desire and direct. We are trying to take care of the whole of the correspondence between Canada and Great Britain, but there is a rule of the Postal Union, to which, of course, we are bound to adhere, under which we are obliged to send the mails according to the direction in which they are routed. With the service we are giving now I am hopeful that all Canadians will help us in this matter by using our service for the transmission of this mail; but we cannot impose it upon them.
So that those who route their letters via New York can have them sent that way?
Undoubtedly.

Mr. Speaker, on rising to resume the debate upon the budget, the adjournment of which I moved on Thursday of last week, I desire to say that it is my intention to present to the House my remarks in the shortest time possible and that I have no desire to extend the debate beyond reasonable bounds.
In reference to the statement made by the Finance Minister (Mr. White) the other day-respecting the financial and material conditions of the country, I am sure that hon. gentlemen upon this side of the House will most heartily joiii with him in felicitating the people of Canada upon the very prosperous conditions which have prevailed throughout this country during the last fiscal year. Increased imports and exports, a buoyant revenue, a great increase in our immigration and commerce, are all indications to a remarkable degree of our prosperity and, I trust, are the tokens of a still greater future for this young country. We, upon this side of the House, followed with oonsid erable interest the successful operation of the many political programmes or policies initiated by the late Government, and I am glad to observe that the continuance of these programmes and policies in the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite, is even productive of good. When hon. gentlemen opposite
Mr. MACDONALD.
were upon this side of the House it was their persistent policy to condemn in the most unmeasured terms practically every-act of the Government referable to trade and financial matters, and at this stage in the career of the present Government, it was only natural to have expected the announcement of something revolutionary with regard to matters relating to trade and finance. However, we find that we have been complimented in the sincerest form of flattery-that is imitation. The Liberal party never pretended to prescribe at any time any administrative or fiscal programme that for long would meet the needs and requirements of this new country, particularly in an age of great progress and change. Liberals, to-day, feel they themselves could improve their own policies to meet changed conditions.
A moment ago I expressed concurrence in the remarks made by the Finance Minister respecting the remarkable, progress this country has made during recent years. I wish to revert to this for a moment just to point out to the House one consideration which I think should never be lost sight of: What is the source of the progress and development which have taken place in this country during the last *decade and more? I submit that such an inquiry is always pertinent, because, if we do not know the spring and source of our development and prosperity, our administrative functions will not be directed in the proper channels, we will improperly ascribe our prosperity and development to wrong sources, and governmental forces will be directed to unprofitable ends. I think that I am merely stating a truism when I say that the prosperity which has been evident in this country in recent years is due to the fact that we are rich in natural resources and, perhaps, to be more specific, I might say, that development and that prosperity are due to the fact that we have had vast areas of fertile lands, that we still have a great reserve of fertile and unoccupied lands and so -long as this condition exists this country is bound to be prosperous. Thomas Carlyle once remarked to an American with whom he was discussing the question of the prosperity of the United States: ' Yo-u may boast of your democracy, or any other ocracy, or any kind of political rubbish, but the reason your country and your folk are prosperous is that you have a vast deal of land with a very few people.' I say, Mr. Speaker, in all confidence, that the prosperity of this country has been due to the fact that we have had, and have, vast quantities of rich lands with a comparatively small population, and that, notwithstanding all our unscientific legislation and other impediments which Parliament and other

causes have east in the way of the progress of the country.
I only desire to emphasize this point for the reason that hon. gentlemen in this House, and others outside, are prone to ascribe the prosperity of this country to this, that and the other reason. I would not presume to say that the development of this country has been due entirely to one cause, but I say that substantially you can trace it directly to the fact which I have mentioned, namely, our great riches and reserves in fertile lands. To that you may trace the large measure of prosperity which we have had in this country in recent years. To it is due our large immigration, the establishment of many homes and the increase in the numbers of producers and consumers. It has been responsible for the increase in the rate of wages more than any other thing, because the agricultural wage in any country always dominates more than any other factor the general wage. It has been responsible for the extensive railway construction which has taken place; it has been responsible, more than any other factor, for the increase in the number, and diversity of the productions of our manufacturers and for the increase of our reserves of wealth.
The House must regret that the budget speech was- not delivered at an earlier period in the session, and disappointment must have prevailed in the country that no important announcement was made by the Minister of Finance respecting tariffs, trade, and markets. There must be in the hon. gentleman's own party many men and many interests who were looking for tariff changes, because the leaders of the Conservative party in 1911, if not directly, then impliedly, must have mortgaged themselves to a very great extent to the representatives of certain interests, who are naturally now looking for the payment of the first instalment on the mortgage. When hon. gentlemen opposite were in opposition they were continually decrying the tariff of the Government of the dav. They stated it was not a tariff suitable to the best interests of the country, and they boasted that were they placed on the treasury benches they would give Canada a tariff which would be more suitable to her needs and which would more rapidly develop her resources and her trade. In what is known as the Halifax platform, one of the several platforms announced by the Prime Minister, he declared the nolicv of the Conservative party upon the tariff question to be:
A fiscal policy which will promote the production within Canada of all useful articles and commodities that can he advantageously produced or manufactured through or by means of our natural resources, having due regard to the interests of the consumer as well as to the just claims of our wage-earning population.
This was a very extensive declaration of policy and it was calculated to meet the demands of any section of the country and any class of interests. If it was meant to be a statement that inherent defects and objections were in the tariff and that the Conservative party were prepared to rectify them when placed in power, then I submit that the Government party have had ample time to implement their pledges in this respect and to make plain what they meant when they asserted that the tariff of the Liberal Government was not one in the interests of Canada.
There are within my knowledge certain things which make me believe, that in 1911 the Conservative party did make promises to many interests respecting tariff changes. In September, 1911, I became aware of the following fact: The Independent Cordage Company was at that particular time, through their regular salesmen, endeavouring to dispose of the products of their factory in Halifax, and on September 1, an order for 150 tons of cordage was placed with the company by one of its usual customers, in Halifax, and which was accepted upon a condition which was stated upon the face of the order:
This order is taken subject to the Government being returned to power. If the Government is defeated we expect the duty to he again placed upon lobster rope.
I know that another manufacturer of cordage obtained an order in Halifax about the same 'time, and a similar condition was imposed. Surely there must have been some promise on the part of the leaders of the Conservative party to the manufacturers of this particular article, that in the event of their coming to power there would be some important change made in the tariff on rope.
I was surprised that the Minister of Finance in his financial statement made no reference to the tariff item dealing with certain forms of rough lumber, which was the subject of discussion last session. I would remind iron, gentlemen that immediately after the Government came to power in 1911, under a ruling of the Treasury Board, made, I suppose, upon the initiation of the Minister of Customs, it was decreed that a duty of twenty-five per cent should be levied upon certain forms of rough lumber imported into this cohntrv wHch previously had been admitted duty free. This matter was brought to the attention of Parliament at its last session by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). On January 23, he moved the following resolution :
That the Minister of Customs, in collecting a duty of twenty-five per cent on sawed planks, boards, joists, scantlings, studding and other 'lumber of wood dressed on one side when the edges thereof are neither jointed,

nor tongued nor grooved, is violating the Customs Act, and unduly and illegally imposing a heavy tax on the people.
When that resolution was under discussion, it was stated by hon. gentlemen opposite that the late Government deliberately and purposely permitted what they termed smuggling of lumber into this country. One of the British Columbia members protested against my denial that, in any event, whether the lumber were properly admitted free or not, it was not a case of smuggling. All hon. gentlemen opposite who participated in that discussion were most emphatic in the contention that lumber importations of that character were properly dutiable. One would have assumed that the Government, having taken that position, would have continued in the imposition of the twenty-five per cent tariff. For some reason, which must appear strange to everybody, the question whether these importations were free or dutiable was referred to the Exchequer Court. I can conceive of nothing that would justify the reference of this question to that court. I think the decision of the Treasury Board was sufficient. The Government could have admitted these importations free, and have given the matter a generous interpretation if they had so wished. The reference to the Exchequer Court was most reprehensible; it was nothing more or less than deliberate waste of public money, and behind it there could have been no real desire on the part of the Government to settle the question upon principle. The Exchequer Court decided that lumber of this character was properly dutiable. Shortly after this decision was given, however, it looked as if an election would take place in the province of Saskatchewan. Somebody suggested that it would hardly do, during an election in that province, to have it said that the present Government, by a decision of the Treasury Board had transferred from the free to the dutiable list certain forms of rough lumber, and that that decision had been endorsed by the Exchequer Court. Something had to be done to relieve the Government from criticism of this nature. What was done? Something even worse than the reference of the issue to the Exchequer Court. An appeal was solemnly made by the Government to the Supreme Court of Canada against a decision of the Exchequer Court, which was in harmony with the decision of the Treasury Board, and which had the endorsement of the Government. Could anything be more reprehensible than that? The Supreme Court of Canada reversed the decision of the Exchequer Court, holding that lumber of this particular character was admissible free of duty. This was not dealing seriously, honestly, and in a businesslike manner with a public matter.
Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
There was no reason in the world for the appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. It was a deliberate and unpardonable waste of public money and a reprehensible trifling with a public matter. It was quite within the power of the Government to interpret generously this tariff item, whatever might be the strictly legal interpretation. The decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, after all, is but a judicial interpretation, and may or may not represent what was the intention of Parliament. Hon. gentlemen opposite said last session that the intention of Parliament was to impose a twenty-five per cent duty on lumber. They asserted that the late Government deliberately and wilfully permitted smuggling of rough lumber into the western provinces, and that officials of the Customs Department deliberately connived at such violations of the tariff. I want to ask the Minister of Finance and his colleagues in the Government if, at last session of Parliament, it was their emphatic and clearly expressed opinion that this lumber should be dutiable at twenty-five per cent, why they have not imposed this twenty-five per cent duty during this session. If they are true to their expressed convictions made to Parliament, they would have this session announced the imposition of a twenty-five per cent tariff upon these importations of lumber. If they say they had no intention or desire to impose a tariff, why do they not amend the tariff so as to make it clear and indisputable that lumber of this particular character might be imported free of duty? Two important courts have disagreed as to the interpretation of this tariff item, and doubt still exists. I submit that the	Government	should
make it absolutely clear, that rough lumber of the character involved, should hereafter be admissible free of duty. The Minister of Finance, and his colleagues must admit that they have not been entirely frank upon this matter.
Before proceeding to discuss the two matters which I have particularly in mind, namely:	the matters of revenue
and expenditure,	I want to	refervery briefly to	one other	matter.A little more than a year ago hon.	gentlemen opposite were telling us that the proper market for this country to seek for its exportable productions was that of the United Kingdom. We were told it was large and not capricious. We were told that the Conservative or Unionist party of England were the advocates of protection and of the giving of a preference to Canada upon her natural products. But certain things have happened during the past few months, and I think we must express surprise that we have heard nothing from hon. gentlemen opposite respecting it. A few months ago the leader of the
Unionist party in Great Britain stated publicly that it was the policy of his party, should they get into power, to give a preference to the natural products of the several dominions of the Empire. Hon. members will recollect that when this statement was made it caused a tremendous hurricane within the Unionist party, practically rending it asunder. Mr. Bonar Law, leader of the Unionist party, then announced that his former declarations would be abandoned, at least as a matter of party policy until after the next election. But that was not acceptable to his political friends, and he was compelled to make a further announcement. He said:
If returned to power, he would immediately impose a moderate tariff on foreign imanufae-tutes and give the dominions a preference ini the British market, the largest preference possible short of the imposition of new duties on food.
That is the last and final statement of the Unionist party in Great Britain upon the matter of preference to the dominions of the Empire concerning which we have heard so much from hon. members opposite for a gTeat many years. Under the policy attributed to the Unionist party some years ago, we were to find ample markets for our exportable products, but apparently all hopes of that have been forever abandoned. Of course, we may possibly be thankful for the fact that, according to Mr. Bonar Law it is possible that, if his party ever does come into power, we may have the chance of exporting to that country our manufactures under some preferential tariff treatment, an advantage which hon. gentlemen in this House will readily perceive, would amount to nothing whatever.
There is just one other matter to which I would refer very briefly at this point, and that is the fact that we have heard nothing this session from the Government or from the Minister of Finance in reference to the appointment of a Tariff Commission. The Prime Minister in 1911, promised that one of the first things he would do if returned to power would be to appoint a tariff commission which should deal with tariff matters in a scientific manner. A Bill to authorize the appointment of such a commission was introduced last session. The Senate made a few 'amendments which did not vitiate the principle of the measure, yet these amendments were refused by the Government, and the Tariff Commission Bill consequently never went into effect. Now, this commission was expected to define a method of placing in the melting-pot all the discordant and irreconcilable facts which are referable always to the making of tariffs, and it was to take therefrom ingots of economic truth which were to satisfy protectionists, freetraders and fair-traders alike . I assume therefor that upon consideration the Government have concluded that a tariff commission could not serve the useful purpose alleged for it prior to the last election. So far as 1 am concerned I do not regret that the measure did not pass and has not been re-introduced. I regard the purpose of a tariff commission as mere fiscal fantasy, and as absurd in its entirety. It was a very good thing with which to humbug the people generally in reference to tariff matters. I could never conceive that it could possibly be of any advantage in the construction of our tariff.
Having said these few words in reference to tariff matters, I desire to discuss briefly some matters relating to revenue and expenditure. it should have been for the fiscal year 1914.
I have pointed out to the House that in the last fiscal year we had a surplus of revenue over expenditure on consolidated fund account of $55,000,000, and in the present year that surplus will probably be $85,000,000 or more. I now wish to discuss briefly this matter and in its relation to taxation. A Government with a surplus of $55,000,000 in the past fiscal year, with a probable surplus during the present fiscal year of $85,000,000 or $90,000,000, can hardly justify its position unless they make a remission of a substantial portion of that surplus to the people. There are two reasons for the ground which I have taken, the one I have given, namely, that we have had for several years past a surplus which in the last year has grown to very substantial proportions and which will be greater still in the next year. There is another reason and it is that we are facing, as people are in most countries, a new problem created by the rapid and abnormal increase in the cost of living. Upon these two grounds I base my conclusion that we have reached the stage when no other course should be pursued by the Government than a remission of taxation.
In order that hon. gentlemen may understand what has been the history of surpluses, or the excess of revenue over consolidated fund expenditure, during the past several years, I would like to give to the House just a few facts upon this point. Let me remind the House that it has been the practice to consider as consolidated fund expenditures only those expenditures necessary to carry on the ordinary affairs of the country, occasionally including some expenditures that might properly be chargeable to capital account. It has usually been agreed by both parties that when it is absolutely necessary that we should embark upon expenditures of a larger and permanent nature, the money required for the same should be obtained by borrowings, and should be charged to what is called capital account. Occasionally that system of financing has been questioned by some people, but on the whole I think the same has met with the favour of hon. gentlemen belonging to both political parties. at one o'clock, I was endeavouring to show reasons why there should be a remission of taxation, the chief one being that ithe Government were taking from the people a greater amount of taxation than the necessary expenditures of the country seemed to justify. I was saying that one of the reasons why I urged that position was that hon. gentlemen opposite, when in opposition, had always contended that continued and large surpluses of revenue beyond necessary expenditure were undesirable and not in the interests of the country. I was about to read some statements made by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) a few years ago, which are particularly referable to this point. I wish to give this as evidence and authority for the soundness of the position I am now taking, namely:	that, by reason of the
immense and extraordinary surpluses which we have had this year and last, there is only one logical and businesslike course for the Government to take, and that is to make a remission of taxation. Speaking in 1905 almost directly upon this point, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce made the following statement:
The axiom is as true as gospel that every dollar of unnecessary taxation you take from the people is so much extracted from their remunerative and productive capital, which otherwise they would employ in the constant processes of production and reproduction.
Upon reference to the words of the hon. gentleman immediately preceding this statement, it will be found that it has particular reference to this matter. Again in 1907, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce,

speaking upon the budget debate, spoke as follows:
The Conservatives in their last years of office preferred to incur a debt of $31,000,000 and leave that extra taxation, which they would have had to take from the people of the country, with the people who need it, and to do with that $31,000,000 of debt what was necessary in the way of capital expenditure to be used and to be enjoyed not only by the people of these years but by the future generations. That is the proper way of, financing. You have no right to take, especially from a young and new, striving and struggling country any great amount more than is needed for the current expenditures of the country. When you are building the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, when you are putting immense public works for the use of the country ' for hundreds of years, why call upon the poor toiling people of one year to put up these works which are to be enjoyed by all generations to come after us?
It will be seen that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was controverting the idea that all capital expenditure should be provided for out of current revenue. The conclusion from that is that the only amount of revenue collected should be that required to meet ordinary expenditures. (Reading):
The proper method is to borrow the money for these capital expenditures and place the burden of interest on each generation which enjoys the use of these permament works. Then those who come after us will pay their proportion of the cost of the works which they are using, and in good time, as the country beeomes wrealthy and able to do so, it can pay off its debt year by year as it pleases. The Finance Minister has made, to my mind, a radical mistake and has done an irreparable injury to this country in his mad race for taxation, and his avoidance of borrowing capital for these capital constructions, consequently drawing from the people their savings ana earnings in larger proportions than he should draw them, and so crippling them to that extent.
This was the judgment of an experienced and highly qualified member and administrator of this Parliament, who takes the position that it is wrong to take from the people that amount of revenue which would meet ordinary and capital expenditures, and further that there should only be taken from the people for revenue purposes that which is necessary to meet ordinary expenditure.
In 1905, speaking upon the same point, the same hon. gentleman said:
Now, my honourable friend-and this is what I want the House to mark-argued that there was a class of expenditure which we ought to charge to capital account. The very moment he argued that and I agreed with him-that very moment he put the strongest argument to this House in favour of keeping your taxation simply up to the limit that is necessary to carry on your expenditures except those which are capital expenditures. But if you keep your capital

I commend these remarks to hon. gentlemen opposite. If they apply the opinions thus expressed to our financial position today, they will conclude that the Government should remit to the people this year a very -considerable sum of money, approximating pretty nearly one-half of the surplus, because as the Minister of Trade and Commerce urged and I think with a great deal of force, particularly so far as this country is concerned-that capital expenditure should not be provided for entirely out of revenue, and that the revenue taken from the people should not exceed, to any great extent at least, the amount of money required for ordinary current expenditures. Therefore I am in a strong position to urge this course upon hon. gentlemen opposite, because they have always taken the same ground, when in opposition, and I think also when they were in power, that is, that it is indefensible, illogical and unbusinesslike to take from the pockets of the people more revenue than was actually required for our ordinary and legitimate expenditures.
Now, I wish to give a further reason wny the Government should not take revenue from the people to an excessive or substantial amount above the ordinary *needs of the country. It is axiomatic that no greater taxation should be taken from the people than is necessary. That is the commonsense theory with regard to taxation, and will meet with the approval of all economists. A British economist once truly remarked:
It is not wise, it is not just, to take from tlie pockets of the people into the treasury of the country an amount greater than the current expenses of the treasury require.
I say further that any taxation scheme that raises a greater revenue than the ordinary expenditure of the country requires does not correspond with the notions regarding taxation commonly entertained by the people of this country. If we go into the provinces, or to the cities and towns of this country, where the collection and disbursements of taxation is un^ler the immediate and direct control of the people, at least to a greater extent than is the case in this Parliament, you find the prevailing idea regarding taxation to be that revenue should be on a parity, or thereabouts, with expenditure. We have, I say, reached a financial position in this country to-day when a remission of taxation must be made, or, in dealing with our financial affairs, we must reverse all preconceived theories and practise regarding finance. The Finance Minister either must remit taxation or must

come to Parliament and state that our revenue is going to be a particular amount; and ask Parliament to provide ways and means of expending it. That hitherto has not been the practice in finance in this or any other country. As I remarked earlier in the day, the practice always has been to estimate your expenditure, as is done in the municipalities, and then provide ways and means for securing the necessary revenue. But here we have reached the position when the Finance Minister must say: Our revenue is growing and will be $75,000,000 or $100,000,000 more than we require for ordinary purposes: come to my aid and tell me how I am going to get rid of this surplus. I must say that his colleagues are displaying considerable capacity in this direction. The estimates presented yesterday indicate great capacity on the part of the Minister of Public Works to expend money. I put the question to hon. gentlemen opposite, whether they consider it good business on the part of the Government they support, to take all the revenue that it can possibly obtain, and then determine how it can be entirely expended.

Another reason why there should be a remission of taxes in view of the large and continued surpluses is that unexpended surpluses are an incentive to governmental waste and extravagance and an encouragement to political corruption. I pointed out to the Minister of Finance last year that he had among his colleagues some extravagant gentlemen, and that they would lead him into unnecessary expenditure. I pointed out that the mere fact that he had such a large surplus-at that time $37,000,-000-would be an attraction to his political friends throughout the country from coast to coast for unreasonable requests for public expenditures. I am sure no one on the other side of the House will more heartily concur in my statement that unexpended surpluses are an incentive to governmental waste and extravagance than my hon.
friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames). He, I' am sure, will take the position he has always taken since he entered Parliament, that the existence of a surplus is a tremendous encouragement to waste. Let me refer the House to the financial history of the United States at a time when they were very much in the same position as we find ourselves to-day. We can frequently study Canadian political and financial problems by reference to the history of the same problems in the United States, for that country is very much like our own, and its people have many of our characteristics and tendencies. In 1887, when Grover Cleveland was President oi the United States, he found himself confronted with a large surplus amounting to $140,000,000. His idea of dealing with that situation was to make a remission of taxation to the people. But the opinion of the Republican party at that time was that the money should be spent rather than that taxation be reduced. There is a very conspicuous similarity between hon. gentlemen opposite and the leaders of the Republican party in this respect. These hon. gentlemen, I have no doubt, will take the position that this Government should spend all the revenue it can get, whether the purposes be profitable or unprofitable. They will take the position that it is not sound finance to reduce taxation whether you need the revenue or not. Mr. James G. Blaine was then in public life in the United States, and he said that rather than reduce taxation it would be better to spend the whiskey tax, which amounted to $69,000,000, on coast protection and divide the balance of the surplus among the different states to reduce real estate taxation. That was what one of the leaders of the Republican party urged; hon. gentlemen opposite are practically coming to the very same position and are urging certain expenditures as unique as the suggestion put forward by Mr. Blain. Mr. Aldridge suggested that it would be wise to purchase United States bonds or make a prepayment of interest rather than a remission of taxation. He did not believe in making a revision of taxation if it could possibly be avoided. Another United States Congressman suggested bounties to wheat growers rather than a remission of taxation, -while another suggested a very elaborate educational scheme. As I said before, President Cleveland recommended a remission or reduction of taxation to the people, and I think his position was sound. He went out of power without being able to effect any substantial remission in taxation, and the Republican party came into power with Mr. Harrison as President. On assuming the presidency, Mr. Harrison found himself confronted with this surplus-and a sur-

plus of revenue must always be the subject of consideration by any government responsible for the administration of public affairs. President Harrison was, as I say, confronted with this plethora of revenue, and he carried out what was the true Republican doctrine, and which I fear is the doctrine of the Conservative party. That doctrine is to expend the surplus; whether the expenditure be wise or unwise, profitable or unprofitable. And what did he do? In the first year of President Harrison's term of office, the amount paid to the people in war pensions jumped from $87,500,000 to $107,000,000, and in his fourth year they had reached the sum of $149,000,000. At the present time I think the pension disbursement in the United States approximates $200,000,000. And what was the cause of the growth in United States pension payments? It was the existence of an annual surplus or a wide margin between revenue and expenditure. Has it been a good thing for the national life of the United States? I believe hon. gentlemen will agree with me that it has had a most disastrous effect upon the national life of the United States. The mere fact that the pensions in that country should to-day far exceed the amount paid ten years after the Civil War is sufficient to condemn and brand the expenditure as corrupt, as indeed, it is. I say that will be the result in this country. Tha Government of this country, enjoying such large and growing surpluses as it has in the past and will have in the future, will be simply opening the door to unwise, unprofitable, and sometimes, corrupt expenditure. There is another reason why I think there should be a remission of taxation. I refer to the increased cost of living. That is not a point which I am going to labour at any great length, for I find I have already taken very much more of the time of the House *than I had intended. I will refer, however, to this phase of modern life in just a few words and I shall be content to state my position in general terms rather than with any particularity. The question of the increased cost of living is a modern one, it affects many countries of the world. I grant you, but nevertheless in this country it is a pressing one and engages the attention of all thoughtful and reflecting men to whatever party they belong. The imperious cry for food at prices within the reach of the ordinary consumer As one that cannot be silenced. The promise of the Creator that the fulness of the earth is for man's enjoyment is one that must be fulfilled, and if its fulfilment is being impeded in any way it is our duty as legislators to remove the impediment in so far as we possibly can.
This question has been studied in recent years in a great many countries and many causes have been assigned for the high cost of living. The causes are not all within the control of Parliament. I do not take such an unfair and illogical position in dealing with this matter. The reasons usually assigned by students of the problem after all are quite few in number and I wish to state some of them. In the first place, it is, I think, granted that oneof the reasons is the increase in the world's production of gold and silver which necessarily and inevitably reduces the purchasing poweT of both gold and silver. Another cause is the waste of nations and in some respects the waste of individuals. Another Teason is the disproportionate growth of urban and rural population. There is an increase in consumption and a higher standard of living adopted by the people of many countries of the world and particularly of Canada. There is the over-expansion of industrial and commercial enterprise, there is the demand for capital, and consequently a very high rate of interest, there is speculative trading and there is also the question of taxation in all its forms. These are some of the causes assigned by students of, the problem, and I suppose each of the causes that I have stated plays its part in some degree or other. But when I have stated the causes it does not in any respect minimise the effects. It is a modern problem thrust upon us for our consideration and action, and we must face and meet the issue squarely. That there has been an increase in this

Should our urban population continue to increase and our rural population continue to decrease proportionately, then the difficulty of meeting the increased cost of living will be accentuated. We will inevitably have an increase in the number of consumers and a decrease in the number of producers, which will intensify the problem -and make it more difficult to solve.
Another aspect of this question should not be overlooked and that is, that wages do not increase proportionately with the increased cost of the necessaries of life, nor do salaries, I mean moderate salaries, increase as rapidly as wages, so that therefore the Increased cost of living 'bears most heavily on the wage-earners and those in receipt of moderate salaries. The social effect of the increased cost of the necessaries of life on the majority of the people of a country, is another factor which enters into the consideration of this question. I shall de-al but briefly with the sociological aspect of the question; and I believe that in the future our political problems will be more sociological than economic, and in that respect the politics of -the future will be in contrast to the politics of the present and of the past. One effect of the high cost of living is to force many men and women into the labour market, it keeps a great number of people upon, and some under the poverty line to an extent that most people do not realize.
I express the hope that during the recess hon.' gentlemen will take the trouble to read the evidence given before the committee dealing with Old Age Pensions, and there they will find startling conditions in this country disclosed. I know that hon. gentlemen will be surprised upon investigation to find how closely, in this new and prosperous country, we approximate the conditions of some of the oldest countries in the world. The existing conditions do not make for physical efficiency; they aggravate the spirit of social unrest and they create new social problems which we must -sooner or later face, and which -are particularly undesirable in a countrv where we have so many avocations which can only be pursued by those engaged in them during certain months of the year. Our climate naturally gives us many occupations which _ are but seasonal. The conditions to which I refer are forcing a grave social as well as economic problem upon us for our consideration. In a general way the modern world has created new conditions which must be faced. In the last analysis it is a human problem and must

be solved in a human way. These conditions are attributable to many causes, some [DOT]of which I grant, are beyond our control; but one of the contributing causes is undoubtedly the question of taxation, wnicn is very largely under our control, at least so far as federal taxation is concerned. These conditions are undoubtedly known to the Government, and the circumstances are such, particularly in view of the large and unnecessary surplus of revenue which the Government are enjoying, that they should face this problem squarely and should grant some relief by a remission of taxation. I think I have made it clear that upon two grounds, namely: that of the great disparity between revenue and ordinary expenditure, which means the extraction of unnecessary taxation from the people, and that referable to the recent increase in the cost of living, there should be made a reduction in taxation.
The hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) asked me if I had any particular method in mind by which this taxation might be reduced. That is a question which might very easily be answered, but in no short time. Hon. gentlemen opposite are responsible to the people of this country for the collection and the disbursement of revenue. After all, I do not think the problem is a difficult one. The fact is that our revenues are in excess of the needs of economical administration, and a reduction is justified to the amount exacted from the people above the requirements of the Government. A reduction in taxation necessarily means a reduction in the amount taken from the people by means of the customs tariff. After the amount of such reduction has been determined, the inquiry follows where it can best be remitted and what articles can best be relieved from taxation in the interests of our citizens. That is the issue which confronts the Government; the responsibility which rests upon the Government and should not' be evaded any longer. I go so far as to say that at the present session of Parliament that responsibility and that duty should have been faced, and that the Government should have declared their determination to make some reduction in taxation at once.

Speaker, I have Jistened with pleasure and attention to the somewhat prolonged remarks of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). I have followed his remarks as carefully as I could, expecting, as his theme developed, that I would find something that might make it possible for me to term his remarks a criticism of the policy of the Government. During the years I have sat in this House, I have never before found the first speech in reply to a budget speech so absolutely devoid of what one might call critical analysis of the position taken by the Government in reference to the subjects treated in the budget speech.
When we rose at one o'clock, I was vainly hoping that my hon. friend would answer the simple question which I put to him whether, in view of his declaration that it is absolutely necessary that there be a remission of taxation, he would tell us how the members on his side _ of the House propose to set about doing it. There are many ways in which it may be done. Many ways have been suggested. I have waited anxiously, presuming that some of these ways would be recommended by the thoughtful and careful member for Halifax. He has avoided, however, disclosing in any way whatever the mind of the Opposition in reference to this matter. One is led to wonder whether the Opposition have a mind on this subject, or whether their mind is so diversified and divided that it is thought the best way is to say simply that something ought to be done, but not to suggest any way in which it might be done.
It is interesting as we take up year by year these matters that are treated in the b iug"t to find how the point of view changes the

remarks of hon. members. Very much that the hon. member for Halifax has said to-day by way of doubting the advisability of the action of the Government has in previous times been alleged from the Opposition benches, and I suppose will continue to be used so long as Parliaments endure. The difference of being a supporter of the Government or a critic of the Government seems to me to leave but little choice of argument, the same stock arguments appear on both sides of the House. I find, for example, that at the present time, what our Liberal friends were accustomed in times past to characterize as 'abundant revenues ' are now spoken of as ' excessive taxation '; and one is hardly nimble enough to be able to adapt oneself to the change of definition. I find, too, that while in times past our Liberal friends were prone to claim for their leader, their Government and themselves credit for Canada's prosperity, growth and power, to-day that is all laid at the door of Providence, and the present Government is regarded as having done but their duty in so far as they have not greatly impeded that manifest development.
The hon. member for Halifax has raised the contention that the present system of taxation is taking out of the pockets of the people of Canada larger sums of money than it is advisable should be collected. His contention is that the people are overtaxed, and therefore he would argue that the system by which these abundant revenues are turned into the public coffers, should be altered in some way which he has not seen fit to define. I want to point out in the first place that the increased revenues are collected entirely by the continuation of the system in force for a number of years, and not changed since the present Government came into power. This proves that, instead of being an extraordinary growth in response to special stimulation, this growth has been the natural, regular, normal. When we find that the system of taxation which has been manifestly sufficient and proper for the past, let us say, twenty-five years, this year yields abundant revenue, I do not think it can be contended that the system, not having been to any notable degree departed from, ought to be altered at this time merely because it does yield abundant revenue. The first question that we have to deal with in taking up the adverse contention of the hon. member for Halifax, namely, that the people are being too heavily taxed, is: Are they being asked to pay more than they can stand ? The sources of our taxation are well known. Roughly speaking, they are divided into three parts. We have no large public enterprises and large federal monopolies as they have in Australia and elsewhere. Only about $30,000,000 of our
revenue comes from sources that are not regarded as taxation, and that amount is counter-balanced by the expenses of the same enterprises against which they are charged. We are generally content in this country, for example, if our post office service manages to make both ends meet. And I doubt very much whether it does make both ends meet, if we charge up against it the subsidies we now pay through the Trade and Commerce Department, the rent of which might properly be charged for buildings, and also the interest on such capital expenditure as might be found necessary from time to time for the extension of the plant. I doubt, were all things taken into account, if there would be a profit in our postal service. So far as our governmental railway is concerned, there were times when we thought that the Government was doing well if it paid expenses. We have improved on that; we are trying to meet not only running expenses, but betterments, repairs and renewals, and even to show what may begin to balance the great interest account, which might fairly be-and is in other countries-charged against government enterprises of that character. But we hardly expect this Government railway, even under its present businesslike management, to reach the point where it can pay expenses, pay for renewals, repairs and betterment, and let us say, three per cent on the $90,000,000 or more invested therein. So, from these accounts the figures very nearly balance. Our main method of collecting revenue is from excise and customs. Now, the excise serves another purpose than raising revenue, for it is largely regulative of certain classes of commodities which, in all parts of the country are to a certain extent, controlled by means of taxation. So that, I think, as the customs tariff raises four-fifths of the money which comes from taxation, probably the reduction which my hon. friend from Halifax has hinted at. but has not very clearly defined, would have to be made on these lines. Let us, then, ask ourselves the question as to whether the customs tariff of Canada as we have it to-day is taking too much out of our people. I would point out that the customs rate as it exists to-day in Canada, is not by any means an unduly high rate, if we compare Canada with other countries where the protective system is considered to have a right of consideration, such countries as Germany, Belgium, France or the United States. We find that, in comparison with these countries, Canada would be reckoned as a low tariff country. Taking the tariff that is levied upon all classes of goods that come into Canada it only averages sixteen per cent of the total value, or taking it upon those goods upon which customs taxes are collected, we find that it falls somewhat

under twenty-six per cent. That is a comparatively low tariff, and if we look into the history of the tariff legislation during the last twenty-five years, we find that under successive governments, whether Conservative or Liberal, there has been a constant tendency for the tariff rate to be reduced. Ever since 1888, it has been by slight gradations, diminishing year by year. In 1888 the rate of duty upon customs paying articles'imported into Canada was 31.858. Then in successive years it fell to 31, to 30, to 29, for a series of years to 27, then to 26, then to 25 and a fraction at the present time, where it has stood for the last two years. So that, with a gradual and falling rate-and probably it will continue to fall inasmuch as some of the recent trade treaties will affect it to a certain extent-with a tariff which compared with other tariffs is low and with a tendency for the rate to gradually fall, it does not seem to me that a strong case can be made out in favour of the contention- if that contention has been fairly put by my hon. friend from Halifax-that our rates of Customs taxation are too high.

I admit that the amount we take from the people of Canada to-day by way of taxation is very much greater than it was in preceding years, but I claim that the shoulders which bear the load to-day are very much stronger than they were in previous years. and two-dollar bills, representing the pocket money of the people, and the change which is constantly passing from one hand to another throughout the country, amounted ten years ago to $11,400,000; to-day we find that $21,000,000 is not more than enough to serve our purposes. Canada's burdenbearing power has increased so greatly during the last ten years that we have no hesitation in making the assertion that it is as easy, if not easier, for Canadians to carry a per capita tax of $17 to-day than it was for them to carry a per capita tax of $8.50 ten years ago.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) is greatly exercised over the fact that we have a surplus, and the burden of his song has, to a large extent, been that the Administration should desire to get rid of the surplus, and that it is dangerous for any government to be entrusted with a surplhs of such a size. I desire to point out, by way of comparison, that it does us good once in a while to see how this lusty young man known as Canada is growing and feeling his strength and power. The Canada of ten years ago is not the Canada of to-day. Ten years ago there was one transcontinental railway, and we were wondering whether we could undertake the building of a second one. To-day we have three transcontinental railroads, nearly completed, each of them opening up vast new territories. We are also expecting to build the Hudson Bay railroad; in fact it is partially finished, and, following out the great development and extension of railroad construction in every province of the Dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific, we find it necessary that large expenditures should be made on ocean terminals. Then, it does not often occur to us to consider how the inhabitable area of Canada has increased during the last ten years. We now have a new Quebec and a new Ontario. I have travelled from one end of the clay belt to the other, and I can say that it is a magnificent agricultural land if climatic conditions are such fas to make it possible for a population there to thrive. In the future the development .and building up of a country 350 miles in length in northern Ontario and Quebec is going to call for large expenditure on the part of the Government. Let us look at the development of the prairie provinces; let us compare the homestead man of ten years ago with the homestead man of to-day. Ten years ago, with the exception of the sections near Winnipeg, Edmonton and Calgary, and a fe.v scattered homesteads along the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway, little or no land was occupied, but, looking at the homestead map of to-day, it is almost impossible to find a spot as large as a postage stamp which has not already keen pre-empted and occupied by farmers

and settlers. The enormous new area which is being opened up in these three provinces will make a great demand upon the expending power of this Government. Then there ia the province of British Columbia, in winch new railroad lines are crossing, like the stripes of the British flag, from northeast to south-west and north-west to southeast, and doubling and trebling the -available area of that province, and all of which will call for vast expenditures.
The hon. member for Halifax has directed attention to what I think will be admitted on both sides of the House to be a growing tendency on the part of the federal government, namely, to assist the provinces in doing what in the earlier days it was considered they should do themselves, out of their own revenues. I would like to point out that in the early days the total revenue enjoyed by all the provinces of the Dominion as compared with the revenue enjoyed by the federal Government was about as one is to two, but to-day the proportion is as one to five. In other words, while the revenue of the federal Government has greatly increased, the revenue of the provincial governments have not, and the provincial governments have demands beyond their ability to pay, while the federal Government is able to cope with all demands made upon it. The result has been that the people of the country have looked more and more to Ottawa and less to their own capitals for assistance in the financial requirements cf their development. That is why Bills are introduced in this Parliament to assist provincial roads and agriculture; that iswhy we find that the various provinces ask for larger subsidies. The federal Government will in the future, no douibt, be asked to enter into further expenditures on 'behalf of the provinces which have hitherto been regarded as entirely provincial, and this will make a further inroad upon the public revenue of the country.
Let it not be forgotten also that the year 1913 marks the 'time when Canada is making her first real expenditure on naval defence. I do not refer merely to the purchase of the three dreadnoughts, but I would refer hon. gentlemen opposite to the outline given by the Prime Minister the other day of the expenditures which will be incumbent upon Canada in the future for her own self-defence; the erection of four dry-docks at the principal ports upon the Atlantic and Pacific coasts; -the establishment of naval bases and their fortification, the development of our fisheries protection fleet and the establishment and maintenance of training schools for sailors and seamen. The Prime Minister the other day made no secret of the fact that the grant of three dreadnoughts would not end the programme of this Government, but that they intended to continue along
other lines in doing what was necessary in many ways and in many places for the defence of Canada, all of which would involve enormous expenditure; so it does not seem to me that we can afford to be ranked among the little Canadians, among those who look back ten years and say we used to spend enough then, can we riot go back to those days and still continue our small expenditure? We are coming to an era of greater things than we have ever known before and the next ten years will probably see a greater advance made by Canada than in any preceding ten years of-her history. We must be prepared to spend what is necessary to develop our country in order that we may be able to deal adequately with the problem which enlarged population and increased development of our resources make incumbent upon us. I shall not be at all surprised if before we celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of Confederation we findthat our annual revenues will considerably exceed $200,000,000 and for the Canada of that time that amount will not be proportionately a greater sum than the revenue of earlier days. I do not see that it would be wise at this time to make an attempt to curtail the revenue coming to us, because we must always be prepared for less prosperous years, we must be prepared for a time when money will not come so freely to us, as it has not come in so freely into Canada this year owing to the high rates of interest; we must be prepared for a time when there may be some check on immigration. While it is easy to cut off sources of revenue, every government knows it is extremely difficult to restore them and consequently it would seem to me to be the path of wisdom to let a normal system which is working reasonably well continue without interference. It is easy to put it wrong, but it will not be difficult to keep it right if it is left alone. I would suggest a remedy for the terrible evils which the hon. member for Halifax dreads. He seems to fear that the greatest possible danger would be large revenue or a surplus. But we have $316,000,000 of indebtedness to work away at in the meantime and if we find ourselves with more money than we know what to do with, it can be used in the reduction of this our debt, and I am sure that no one will say it is not wise policy in times of plenty to pay your debts and reduce your obligations because the times may become harder, when it will be necessary to increase your indebtedness.

But when the revenues are abundant, it is much more difficult to say no and there are many who are always ready to make plausible suggestions as to how money may be expended so that a Finance Minister who can keep well within his revenues in a flourishing year is certainly deserving of great credit.

Some of the short term obligations contracted at high rates of interest have fallen due, and the $23,300,000 we had in hand has been used in paying off debts running at three and a quarter and four per cent interest, which means that altogether we will start out in 1913-14 with a necessity of appropriating, in order to meet the interest on the public debt of the country, some $900,000 less than we had to appropriate a year ago. That $900,000 is so much saved money, it is so much to our advantage. It, therefore, has been a very fortunate circumstance that our Finanoe Minister has been able to look ahead, has been able to realize that this year was going to be a bad one for borrowing, has been able, instead of incurring large amounts of indebtedness at high rates of interest which would have to be paid by succeeding generations, to live within his revenue without incurring another dollar of debt and to take up the high interest bearing obligations to the extent of $23,000,000 and thus reduce our annual interest charges by nearly $1,000,000. Then, too, he has been able to sustain the credit of the country by coming to the rescue of the Grand Trunk Pacific and buying the bonds issued by that railroad so that they might not be put upon the market and sold at a reduced figure. In that way our credit as an endorser has been preserved. I think you may safely say that, although the past year has been one of considerable money stringency in certain money markets of the world, Canada stands today in a better financial position in those markets than she ever occupied at any time before in her history.
Now, I want to congratulate the country generally also upon the fact that the trade figures for the past year are on the whole thoroughly satisfactory. For the first time in the history of Canada we have reached high-water mark and passed it- I mean the billion-dollar mark as the total of our imports and exports for the year. I admit that the balance of trade is against us. I admit that at first glance one might say that to have sixty-four per cent of imports as against thirty-six per cent of exports was not a healthy sign. But it must be remembered that Canada is a very rapidly growing and expanding country. We are exactly in the position of a manufacturer who, seeing his business greatly extended, determines to put a new wing on his factory. While he is building that new wing he is paying out large sums of money for bricks, mortar, planking, machinery, roofing, and everything that goes into that structure. Consequently you take a balance sheet for the year and what do you find? You find that the produce does not begin to pay for what

he has consumed. He may have borrowed that money, or the money may have been put into the business by some one else. But his products are not equal to his consumption because he is extending his business. That is what we are doing in Canada and the idea could not be better expressed than it is in a statement in the Canadian Year Book under ' Wholesale Prices ' republished from the Toronto Globe. The extract is as follows:
Our new labour is employed as largely upon the construction of the machinery with which we shall presently increase enormously our output of goods, as upon the production of food stuffs which would have an immediate revenue value, and this circumstance would intensify the effect of any serious slackening in our construction operations.
In other words, we are in the position that I have described of preparing for greater things. We are squaring our shoulders, we are buying new tools, we are enlarging our production and we expect to do a very much bigger business because of the fact that in a short time we shall have largely increased our plant.
Did we find a state of affairs such as we see in older countries where the exports and imports were exactly balanced, we would say that Canada was stationary, and we would be right in saying so because it would mean that we had reached the point of equilibrium and that expansion, growth and preparation for future increase were no longer in evidence. I admit that our market to the south of us is not taking as large quantities of Canadian goods as sometimes it is argued that market should. I think that our American friends are themselves preparing to make it possible for Canada to send more to them than we have been sending, but as matters have stood in the past the fault has not been ours, but that of our friends in the United States, because they have had towards us a tariff wall twice as high as we have had towards them. An analysis of the articles which we do send to them shows that they only take from Canada such raw materials as they can themselves work up and make a substantial profit upon. Our exports to the United States last year amounted to $113,000,000 and of this sum $67,000,000 represented minerals, coal and wood in unmanufactured form. Besides that the only other items of importance that we exported to the United States were breadstuffs, fish, hay and hides. At the present time the Americans take from us mainly our raw materials and, in order to make a profit, they manufacture them, export them and 'compete with us in the other markets of the world. It would therefore not be a very great loss to us if the amount of that export did not increase so long as it kept to
raw materials of that character because we would ourselves manufacture them and make a reasonable profit out of them.
I also would like to congratulate the Government upon the wonderful showing that the Immigration Department has made during the last year. There again we have reached the high water mark which will stand as a record in the future. Four hundred thousand people have been added to our numbers during the year which has just ended. I do not think that we realize what our problem of assimilation is and how much greater it is than have ever been the problems of similar nations elsewhere. At the time when the United States had iso,000,000 population, they were only taking 'in about four times as many people as we are to-day. We, with a population of 8,000,000, are adding one-twentieth to our population annually by immigration. There never was a time in the history of the United States when they added more than one-fortieth or one-fiftieth to their population in any given year. We have to address ourselves to the solution of this great problem of taking care of the immigrants that come to Canada. But certainly it is an indication of the attractiveness of 'Canada and of the way in which our prosperity is challenging the attention of the world. in Teply to what the hon. member said regarding the high cost of living. I do not think he made his case very strong in endeavouring to prove that the taxation at present being taken from the country was the reason for the high cost of living. It may be an incident to it, but he has only to look around the world to see that the high cost of living is general. He will find it in protected countries and unprotected countries just the same; he will find it in Great Britain where since 1897 the cost of the foodstuffs of the British workingman has increased fifty per cent; he will find it in the United States; he will find it elsewhere. If he could point out to me that only in high tariff countries the cost of living had gone up and that in low tariff countries or countries that have no tariff it had remained stationary, I would see the force of his argument. But as the matter stands, I cannot see that it is more than an incident and not the real cause. If you come to consider the conditions in Canada you will find that the high cost of living is largely due to the fact that our consumptive power has increased more rapidly than our productive power. Think that over for a moment and you will see that the demand has increased more rapidly than the supply in the Canadian home market and the effect of course is that products have advanced in price.
We export a great deal.

We export a great deal of
raw material. Would the hon. gentleman undertake to curtail the demand and so lessen the Canadian market by bringing in the cheap-made products of elsewhere and then say: as we have lessened the demand the local supply can take care of the balance and consequently prices may be expected to fall? Is not that a pretty dangerous experiment? If we follow a path of that kind may we not find ourselves far worse in the last result than in the first, because we are deliberately introducing a method whereby we are curtailing the purchasing power of a portion of the Canadian people, and once you take that power from them it is difficult to restore it? Let me use an illustration: suppose there is a town in the West with fifty families and there is in the immediate neighbourhood one hundred farmers, who are supplying them with the necessities of life, and prices are fairly normal. But suppose the town rapidly increases from fifty families to two hundred families and the farmers in the immediate neighbour hood have a larger market for their products than before and not enough to supply it, the result would be for the time being that prices would go up and would continue at a high level until the hundred farmers producing became two hundred and the supply and demand were equalized. You will find that is the history of what i3 working all the time. Prices go up because the demand increases more rapidly than the supply. When the supply overtakes the demand, there is a tendency towards equilibrium. That I think will come here as elsewhere, if we only have patience. To my mind it would not be wise, for the sake of a possible temporary relief, to interfere with that system. If we do that, we would find ourselves cutting off from a large proportion of the Canadian people the purchasing power which it is extremely' valuable and necessary for them to have.
I have been wondering whether my hon. friend from Halifax was going to intimate that there might be certain articles, on which taxation is now levied by way of customs duty, that might be put on the free list. Is that his method of reducing taxation? He has not disclosed any method to us. There again let me point out, in order that it may be clearly in our minds, that in the argument raised we are taking what used to be known as ' the vicious circle.' Protection is not justifiable for one unless it is justifiable for all. If it is not justifiable for one, it is not justifiable for all. All of us are producers and consumers alike. You cannot say to one producer: You are not entitled to protection, and then say to another producer: You are entitled to protection. Consequently if protection exists in any country, it must be distributed with fairness and equality to all those industries throughout that country which the Government judge to be entitled to receive

it. Suppose you say to an industry: The demand for a reduced rate on the article you produce is so great that we have decided that your industry shall be the victim and that you will hereafter be subject to world-wide competition. Take, for example, an article of which I know nothing, but which I may perhaps use for purposes of illustration, namely: shovels. Suppose the price of a shovel in Canada is claimed to be too high, and you say: The man who uses a shovel must have it at a lower rate. Therefore we will take off the duty on shovels and allow them to come in from the whole world in order that the price may fall. What would be the result? The men in Canada who are making shovels would probably find themselves out of business by reason of ruinous competition. Their employees would find themselves out of employment and would go into other industries at lower wages. They would be discontented. They would say: If the industry which I am accustomed to work at is no longer protected, why should I pay for meat and lamb and dairy products that are raised by protected farmers? I refuse to do so. Suppose his refusal can be put into actual effect, and the farmer finds that his products are to be no longer protected. He will say: Why should I pay protected rates for my coat and hat and boots and shoes and so on? The moment you let in the principle that it is possible to single out one man and say to him that his protection shall cease henceforth, it seems to me you will find no place where you can stop until' the whole protection is taken away.
That is the doctrine.

If that is the doctrine which hon. gentlemen opposite wish to adopt, I shall be delighted to deal with it. If the hon. member for Halifax had intimated a list of articles that he would like to see sacrificed and thrown to the wolves, let us say, we would have been delighted to deal with those articles. Striking in the dark as we are at the present time, we can only enunciate the general principle, and intimate -that protection, if it is to be maintained, is right for one and right for all, and that consequently an infringement upon it brings danger to all.
