No allowance has been made for charity, churches, pleasure, sickness, drugs, medical attendance or tobacco. After the figures I have given and comparisons I have made, it is needless to go into statistics regarding the earning power of work-331
men in these three respective cities, for some can be found in the remarks I made last year. But if we compare the increase in the cost of living in twelve months we come, to our astonishment, to a difference of twenty-two per cent in Montreal alone, and no doubt it has increased in the same proportion in other cities.
The causes for such an increase may be many, or few. Every day we hear of new causes, and all of our great economists do not seem to agree on the real cause of such an alarming increase. Some will say that the production of gold has something to do with it. Others will say that scarcity of grass in our fields is responsible also. Others will say that the cost of transportation is the great plague. The duplication of services in connection with the distribution of goods, which increases more and more every day, is also responsible. By the words ' duplication of service,' I mean the delivery at the consumer's door not only of all that he eats and drinks, but also of every minor .article purchased by him at the city or village store. Many other causes too numerous to mention are also assigned for the high cost of living.
It is strange, however, that very few men who make a special study of this great problem have counselled the cutting out of the middleman's profit, and the more we study this great question the more we conclude that the tariff has everything to do with this increase, which has become a plague. Observing conditions from a practical point of view, I have no hesitation in saying that over-capitalization, better known as watered stock, is absolutely responsible for the tariff and therefore responsible for the increased cost of living. This year we can anticipate that no less than two hundred and fifty mil-ions will be paid as interest on watered stock alone. If we compare this enormous interest paid, with the population in Canada at the present time, say, 7,500,000 inhabitants, we find that about $33.30 is imposed on every man, woman and child in the country, or in other words $166.50 per family, and we must not lose sight of the fact that they have no choice as to whether they shall pay or not. I call this highway robbery, for it is impossible under present conditions to prevent this operation and we must accept it.
If we proceed further with our investigation and subtract the number of inhabitants that cannot be called upon to pay this over-tax, it becomes more alarming. About ten per cent of our population come under this category. There are the patients in all of our institutions, the invalids, also a large number who will never work, without mentioning the parasites, who are more dangerous

to society than all other classes combined. Deducting the ten per cent I have already mentioned are the population upon which this burden is really imposed is then 6,750,-0O0,fand the amount would be $37 on every individual or $185 per family. This is too heavy a tax, especially when it is paid on a fictitious and non-existent value and this situation is responsible for the increased cost of living and it also contributes to the increase of the tariff. In other words, it furnishes arguments for high protectionists in favour of not reducing or abolishing the tariff on first necessities of life.
I would like to read here an expression which appeared in the Monetary Times of October 12, 1912, on this subject, and the expression in such a paper surely will be accepted in this House. This expression although given by an American covers the situation m our own country.
The rise in the cost of living is still a problem on the North American continent. It has increased sharply during the recent year' and is still rapidly rising. Mr. J. J' Hill has said that the cost of high living has been an important factor: in other words that extravagance is one of our faults. While there is much truth in that assertion, inquiries prove that, aside from reckless expenditures, the cost of necessaries has risen con-eider ably. In addition, the average income has not increased to a corresponding degree. There has just been completed under the aus-Pv0eSn0^ United States Labour Bureau of the Department of Commerce and Labour, a survey of retail prices actually paid by consumers of the cities of the country.
The statistics of this survey, when used along with the report of the 1910 census, shows that the average workingman conld, in 1909, buy with the results of a day's labour less than nine-tenths of the food he could buy with his day's labour in 1899. By a conservative estimate, he can to-day buy less than four-fifths. Without any indulgence in high living, the cost of duplicating a wholesome weeks regime in 1899 is to-day fifty-two to seventy-seven per cent higher than it was then, and even if a man gets twenty-five per cent more wages than he got then he is still twenty-one per cent worse off on his bill for meats and groceries.
This is a considerable rise for a period covering ten or a dozen years; but the grade that prices have taken in their upward course is steeper now than it has ever been before in the period. The Government's figures show that, between June 15, 1911 and June 15, 1912, prices of ordinary food increased six to ten per cent.
Undoubtedly similar conditions, generally speaking, prevail in Canada, for it would appear that all employers of labour have not yet shouldered their share of the difficulty. I would like to cite an item that appeared in the Montreal Gazette of Mr. VERVILLE
November 22, 1912, a newspaper in which members on the other side of the House have absolute confidence. I quote:
A man in Winnipeg the other day bought a barrel of Ontario apples paying therefor $5.25. In it he found a note from the grower of the fruit, which read:	' I got
seventy cents for this barrel of apples, what did you pay for it '. . . . The $4.55 difference between the purchaser's price in this case presumably went part to the original buyer as profit, part, possibly almost a dollar, to a railway company for hauling it twelve or fourteen hundred miles, and part as profit to the Winnipeg merchant who sold and delivered it. There is money madd somewhere in the handling, if not in the growing of apples.
What is said of this barrel of apples can be said of all commodities and especially of foodstuffs, and the Montreal Gazette simply states the facts. But if we go deeper into this case we can specialize and probably conclude who gets the difference, for the same paper in its issue of November 27, 1912, five days later, published a small article in its editorial columns from the Winnipeg Telegram which reads:
The Winnipeg Telegram is trying to figure out how it is that a barrel of apples for which an Ontario farmer received 70 cents, retails in Winnipeg at $5.25 without somebody or other making enormous profits. The freight is 76 cents per barrel and the barrel itself cost 30 cents, a total cost of $1.76 for the fruit laid down in Winnipeg. This leaves $4.95 for somebody so far unknown. Having failed to locate the whereabouts of the discrepancy the searcher might try something easier. In the case of a potato shipment from Stonewall to Winnipeg, a distance of 20 miles, the farmer it appears got 30 cents a bushel; the freight was 3i cents a bushel, the potatoes sold at wholesale at 55 cents at Winnipeg, and the local consumer paid 65 cents.
The producer an-d the railway received practically one half that amount for grow-lng the bushel and carrying it to the market. Who got the rest of the 65 cents?
It seems from these figures that the farmers and the consumers ought to be up in arms against such exploitation. The farmers, the great producers of natural products, should understand that they, as well as the masses in the cities, are the tools of the combines, and that when an open market is offered to them that they should grasp the opportunity to bring about better conditions. It is unfair for the farmer or fruit grower to support those that are responsible for such conditions. The farmers are not getting the full value of their products, and we, in the cities, are paying too much. It is time also that the farmers of the country should understand that they are the consumers of all that is produced in the cities. What has been said of apples or of potatoes can also be

said of all other goods they have to purchase.
If the farmers of the country would take the trouble to prepare their budget and classify the different items on which they have to pay exorbitant prices, as well as high tariffs, they would conclude that after allowing a good substantial profit to the manufacturer as well as the wholesaler, retailer, and the transportation companies, they are paying all the way from 22 to 40 per cent higher than they should pay and without a particle of benefit to them.

There were in December last in storage approximately 1,800,000 dozens of eggs which have been bought from farmers or shippers for 18 to 20 cents per dozen. After those eggs have been in storage from six to seven months they are put on the retail market at 35, 40 and as high as 60 cents, according to their quality after classification. The eggs are tested when entering and retested in the fall of the year. The labour upon the two tests amounts to two-thirds of a cent per dozen eggs. The storage for the season is one and one-third cents per dozen, making a total of 22 cents, including insurance. The retailer receives as profits from three to four cents per dozen, making 25 to 26 cents a dozen. The difference between 25 cents and an average of at least 45 cents leaves a net profit of 80 per cent. It.may be said that there must be a large number of eggs which are not fit for consumption. It would reasonably appear so, but they have found another way of putting them on the market, and here I will explain their mode of operation. When eggs are tested for the second time, those supposed to be unfit for consumption, and I may say, half rotten, are handled in a very cautious manner. Half of an egg may be very bad and the other half not very good. I will now give some information on another product which is also of great importance. Chickens are bought in the best part of the season from the farmers at 8 to 9 cents, turkeys at 12 to 14 cents, and geese at 7 to 8 cents a pound.
After entering the storage, these products are frozen and kept there at the cost of three-eights of a cent for each subsequent month, the total cost being half a cent. Chickens thus cost say 81 cents and are sold on the retail market at 18 cents per pound, the profit of the retailer being about 3 cents per pound. This gives to the storage company about 70 per cent net profit.
For turkeys an average price of 13 cents is paid. They go through the same process, and, by allowing 3 cents to the retailer, the net price becomes 161 cents. They are sold on the markets at 22 cents, making a net profit of 50 per cent. For geese an average price of 71 cents is paid. They go through the same process, and by allowing 3 cents to the retailer, the net price becomes 11 cents. They are sold on the market at 16 cents, making a net profit of about 50 per cent. It must be borne in mind that the profit here allowed the retailer is generous enough, as it is above 40 per cent; I am sure that there are very few, if any, who are making that much.
I have also been informed that thousands of pounds of these foodstuffs, after having been kept in storage for two or three years" are so unfit for consumption that they have to be thrown away as garbage, and that to the knowledge of the operators alone. We must also remember that if these commodities are kept for that length of time the prices will be increased; that the storage companies by so doing can later on sell at exorbitant prices and make a profit of from one hundred to one hundred and fifty per cent, but in more than one case they have had to throw away products that should have been sold in the proper time, and

which would then have been substantial food for the public.
Present economic conditions do not permit the rank and file to buy luxuries in foodstuffs, but instead of giving the people a chance to feed themselves at a reasonable price, these companies prefer to throw this food away. I would ask the members of this House who belong to the medical profession if it is any wonder that there now and then appear in different forms diseases which out most eminent men are making strong efforts to put down and prevent. I desire here to give some figures establishing the prices paid to the fishermen by proprietors of cold storage warehouses and the prices paid by the consumers. We must admit that prices paid to the producers may vary according to sea-son and supply. Continued rough weather may prevent the fishermen from reaching the fishing grounds, thus creating a shortage in the supply of fresh fish, when the prices to the producer may slightly increase. But if we take the average price paid to the fishermen, we find that they receive 14 cents per pound with entrails removed. This price is paid for cod, haddock, cusk and hake, which are retailed at 5 cents per pound, a difference of 350 per cent, and steak out from large fish of the above varieties sells as high a-s 124 cents per pound. I am in doubt -as to the retailer making more than 2 cents per pound profit. No. 1 fresh mackerel, were bought l-ast -summer from the fishermen for 10 cents each, and sold to the consumers for 30 cents, a difference of 200 per cent. I have mentioned New York state. It is perhaps interesting to have some information concerning . the cost of standard living in New York city. I have given figures and made comparisons from that city. Let me now compare the standard of living in New York with the standard of living in Montreal, and you will see that the cost is far cheaper in New York than in the Metropolis of Canada. The New York state conference on charities and correction through their investigation, and it was an elaborate one, came to the conclusion that $825 per year was the necessary income to allow a family to maintain a fair and proper standard of living in New YTork city. If we compare these figures with those I have already given on food stuffs in Montreal and New York the working men of the Canadian Metropolis should receive ninety-five per cent more wages to enable them to balance their budget. The minimum itemized estimate established by that conference is $709.20 for a family of five. The figure I gave last year for Montreal was $746.13, and if we compare the earning power of working men, we find that New York has an advantage of sixty per cent over Montreal. I have not yet found in the labour ranks a mathematician clever enough to solve this problem. This House is composed of members of high standing, many of whom are great financiers and I call upon them to solve it.
The coal famine, if it can be called such, this year furnishes an occasion also for the legislators of the country to take necessary steps to prevent its repetition next year. We are informed, and rightly so, that coal has cost very little more a ton to the operators this year than last year; nevertheless, the coal was sold during the latter part of December, 1912, at $J0 per ton. The profit made at $7 and $7.50 per ton was enough to enrich to an alarming proportion operators of mines and also the wholesale dealers. This increase of about forty per cent to those who have revenues enough to buy by the ton and for cash on delivery may not be a burden. What about the amount paid by the largest part of the consumers? With such an exhorbitant price they have to buy in small quantities, by the basket or by the 100 pounds. Has any one in this House ever dreamt

what it costs for coal under the present conditions to the poorer classes of people who are in the majority in this country? They have to pay from seventy-five cents to one dollar per one hundred pounds; this would mean $15 to $20 per ton, or in other words, 100 to 155 per cent more than they could buy their coal for last year. Such an exorbitant price this year has forced the masses to buy by the hundred pounds instead of by the ton. Of course, the wholesaler will say that he is not responsible for such a charge, but he has cornered the coal market and has been successful in driving the small coal dealers out of business, thus increasing the power of exploitation of the coal trust.
Some few years ago, the statement was made that the strike of the coal miners was responsible for the increase of coal. Information at my command proves that not more than eight cents per ton has been added to the. cost on that account. It is a wonder that the trust this year does not use the same argument, for the coal trust has mo more sense of honour than any other institution of the same character. I -am informed that coal costs $2.50 per gross ton, free on board, in the cars at the mines. The freight on a car is $2.76 per ton, thus making the value of the coal delivered in Montreal $5.26 per ton. By tallowing a reasonable profit to the wholesaler, say, one dollar per ton, and a legitimate profit to the retailer, say, one dollar per ton, the coal can be delivered in every workingman's cellar for $7.26 per ton. The prices charged in December were $10 and $11 per ton. If the prices of last year, $7 and $7.50, were high enough to enrich the operators and wholesalers to an alarming proportion, what about the profits this year?
If we take the population of Montreal, say, 550,000 and divide by 5 as to families, we have then 110,000 families at an average of three tons, which is too little. This makes
440,000	tons of coal for consumption in that city alone -and for the winter only. A reasonable average would be 450,000 tons, and by giving a good substantial profit to all those who handle coal we can figure that the trust has pocketed this year at least over and above a legitimate profit $1,125,000, or, at the rate of five toms per family, $1,375,000.
Is this not enough to justify us in asking that such -a proceeding should be prevented? Is this not enough to arouse the masses against conditions that permit such exploitation? Is this not enough to cause the rank and file to protest, because after being robbed of their food, they are also robbed of their means of keeping warm in winter. If the members of this House had to submit for a few Mr. VERVILLE.
days to the same privation that a great number of workingmen had to submit to on account of the exorbitant price of coal last winter, I am convinced that Bills would be introduced or the Government would be obliged to legislate for the prevention of such disastrous operations.

What Coal Companies did. Took $13,450,000 from Consumers to pay $4,000,000 Wages.

Hard coal companies increased the wages of their employees at the rate of $4,000,000, according to a report based on an investigation by the Bureau of Labour submitted to the House to-day.
The report submitted by Secretary Nagel is the result of an investigation concluded in response to a House resolution asking for the ' elements of cost and profit included in the present high price of anthracite/
An average increase of 26 cents a ton in) wholesale coal prices was discovered to have been made since the strike agreement of last May. In spite of the fact that the workers benefitted about $4,000,000 in increased wages during the year, the report adds that ' the recent increases in prices have been more than sufficient to compensate fully those companies whose cost of production have increased most rapidly during recent years, and at the same time have very greatly increased the profits of those companies, of whom there are at least several whose costs of production either decreased or remained stationary during the same period/
On more than $13,000,000 gained by the operators after the strike agreement, $10,900,000 was derived from general increase in prices and about $2,500,000 from the suspension of April and May discounts, while in addition a limited number of operators are reported bo have ' received very large sums through the sale of coal at premiums made possible by the shortage of shipments/ incident to the strike. As a matter of principle, it is not a bad thing for consumers to attempt to defend themselves against the increase of prices.
If the householders of the departments of the North of L'Aisme and others, when clubbing together and making revendica-tions, had contented themselves with boycotting certain traders or certain marketers and had refrained totally or at least partially during a few days from purchasing goods at exorbitant prices, they certainly could not be blamed for doing so; on the contrary, they would have been worthy of praise.

The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) has given us a very long discourse presumably in the interest of the labouring classes. I myself represent a labouring constituency and I should 'be very sorry indeed for the lot of the workingman, if I thought that many of the statements the bon. gentleman has placed on ' Hansard ' were in any sense true or could be borne out by facts. The figures that he has quoted with regard to the necessities of life, particularly with regard to fruit, vegetables and dairy products, may apply to some hole or corner in the Dominion of Canada, but in no sense can be said to represent what the average workingman of Canada has to pay for these products. He made the broad statement in the early part of his address that the cost of living in Montreal is practically one hundred per cent higher than in New York. I wonder how many citizens of Canada the hon. gentleman expects to believe such a statement. I believe he said also that Montreal was eighty per cent higher in cost of living than Chicago. The figures he quoted on some ordinary necessaries of life it is unnecessary for me to spend even a moment in recounting, because they bear their refutation on - their face; they are absolutely not in accord with the facts well known to the workingmen whom he presumes to represent. The workingmen of Canada are in no such disposition as he has given us to understand. The city from which I come, is not a large city, having a population in round figures of 25,000, of whom 7,000 are classed as workingmen and working in the factories of that city, and before I get through I shall endeavour to show what they are producing and how they are living. But the hon. gentleman has made broad statements and I think it a pity that such statements should go on ' Hansard ' uncontradicted, because they are absolutely untrue in regard to the large majority of products which are usually classed as necessities of life. It may be that Ontario differs from Quebec in that respect. The factories of Ontario are located largely in agricultural centres, and it is well known by everyone who frequents the markets of the various towns and cities of Ontario that the prices that obtain there-and I call the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) as a witness-are very moderate indeed, and not more than from twenty-five to fifty per cent

of those the hon. member for Maisonneuve has just stated. It was to be expected that when he made the statement that there was great unrest and disquiet in Canada among the workingmen, he would have given a few facts to bear out that'statement. I take the ground that the workingmen of Canada are thrifty, prosperous and contented. I think that statement cannot be refuted. In order to prove it let me give a few figures. I take the facts of industrial disputes for 1911, the last year for which I have such figures at hand. In that year there were one hundred industrial disputes in Canada. Of these, forty-two were settled between the parties, two were settled by arbitration and seven by conciliation. In seventeen cases work was resumed on the employers' terms: in ten cases, the strikers places were filled. Of the total, thirty-four ended favourably to the employers, twenty-one favourably to the employees, and there were compromises in twenty-four. That surely does not show great dissatisfaction among the workingmen of Canada; it shows that the workingmen are well satisfied with their lot. Let me give the returns for the past ten years in order that there may be no misunderstanding as to how many industrial disputes we have had, and as to whether or not the workingmen are satisfied with present conditions. The total number of disputes that we have had during the ten year period between 1902 and 1911 was 1,069, nearly all of them in Ontario. My hon. friend who has just spoken has attributed many of the disabilities under which the workingmen of Canada labour to the fact that we have a tariff in Canada, and he endeavoured to show that the existence of this tariff was raising the price of goods to the extent of one hundred per cent in Montreal. or Chicago. I think, therefore, that the ground upon which the hon. gentleman based his argument is entirely fallacious, and that the workingmen of Canada are well satisfied with their lot. compete with the world in quality and_ in price. I am asked whether agricultural implements should not stand a reduction so that the farmer would get his implements cheaper. I say at once that I believe they would under certain conditions, but if this country should embark upon the conditions which I shall name, I think they would be doing a very unwise thing. To reduce largely the duty on agricultural implements, which is now from fifteen per cent to twenty per cent, would mean that you would hit probably fifty or one hundred subsidiary interests that produce the raw material of which the agricultural _ implements turned out by these factories are composed. You certainly could not reduce the duty on the implements without reducing the duties on the raw material which enters into their manufacture.

Do the manufacturers
not get a rebate of ninety-nine per cent?

Only on reapers and mowers. They receive a refund on export of ninety-nine per cent of the duty paid, one per cent being retained for collection and redistribution, but only in the case of mowers and reapers are any concessions made with regard to the raw material that enters into their manufacture. That concession was made because the duty was reduced some two and one-half per cent years ago by the Government of which my hon. friend was then a supporter. So I think that it would only be possible to reduce the duty on agricultural implements if the accessory parts entering into the manufacture of the goods were made subject to the same concession. These materials would include iron and steel goods, bolts, screws, bars, angles, paint, varnishes, and everything entering into the manufacture of that line of goods. Therefore if that reduction were effected, instead of penalizing just a few manufacturers of agricultural machinery, you would hit forty, fifty or one hundred industries which manufacture the various materials entering into the construction of these implements. In my judgment we are not hitting the farmers by the high duty. The implements in Canada to-day are sold as cheaply as in any country in the world, with the exception of the United States. It has been charged that these goods are being sold cheaper in England than they are in Canada, but I have figures to refute that assertion.

Why does production
cost less in the United States than in Canada?

Where Canada has a million dollars employed in the agricultural implement business, the United States probably has fifteen or twenty millions. The International Harvester Company has probably more capital engaged in the implement manufacturing business than all the implement manufacturers of the Dominion. Their production is enormously large; everyone knows that in order to have goods turned out efficiently and at the lowest possible cost, they must he manufactured in large quantities. Therefore all the small dealers and manufacturers have gone to the wall under recent competition. Hon. gentlemen may say that the manufacturer is making too much money, but the fact remains that all the small men have been driven out of business by the fierceness of home competition. About thirty years ago there were twenty-five different kinds of binders and reapers manufactured in the Province of Ontario alone; how many are there to-day? Three. What has become of the rest? They have all been driven out of business by the fierceness of home competi-
Mr COCKSHUTT.
tion and by the large production of the few manufacturers who have been enabled, by [DOT]the use of larger capital, to turn out a thousand machines where the small man turned out only ten. I am not speaking at the instigation of any single manufacturer, hut I say that if every branch of industry in Canada were as efficiently managed and turned out goods as cheaply as the implement manufacturers, there would not be much cause for complaint. I say that, knowing it to be absolutely by the book. Although hon. gentlemen opposite may think that we are hard-hearted wretches to pursue those who do not pay up I can tell the country why our goods are not sold even cheaper to-day to Canadians. The terms of credit are entirely out of proportion to what they should be and are probably in excess of almost any country in the world. Six months is considered a very short time. Agricultural goods run from six months to two tyearS credit and this year only about forty per cent of collections have been collected and yet hon. gentlemen think we are hard-hearted because we ask that occasionally these accounts should he paid up.

The hon. member says
that the terms are from six months to two years, after six months the manufacturers charge interest do they not?

That is altogether by arrangement. If the hon. gentleman is referring to a man who wants to buy at six months credit, the exact price is named at the time of the purchase. Many men want to buy on two to four payments fixed over a period of from six months to two years. Of course, after six months, interest is charged in those cases, but there is a cash price also quoted; if the man wants to buy for cash he gets a liberal discount.
How much?
From five ner cent to ten per cent on the average and on large orders such as are placed by some farmers in the West who buy in quantities there is a still more liberal discount.

It is impossible for me to get a better discount than six per cent per annum, no discount of five per cent or ten per cent but a discount of six per cent per annum. That is to say, I can buy a binder to-day dated in October. I can pay for it any time in October, but if I buy if for cash I get a discount of six per cent per annum.

Mv hon. friend is
speaking from personal experience and I cannot say whether he is correct, but I am speaking of the western trade.
I am speaking from experience and experience with the Massey Harris Company.

Of course I am not posted as to the terms on which the Massey Harris Company do business and, therefore, cannot say what they allow, but in round figures, I think, I can say five per cent to ten per cent discount can be got from any agricultural implement dealer if a man wishes to pay cash.
That is all I could get. I offered to pay cash and the only discount I could get was six per cent per annum, and that was not sufficient to induce me to pay cash as I had to pay that for money.

Another reason why implements are higher than some of our friends think they should be is on account of the high cost of transportation. If my friends only knew the cost of getting these goods here out to the West and distributing them into the various business centres they would see that a large part of the cost of machinery is made up of transportation charges. I have in my hand a few of the freight rates charged on a reaper to certain points from Toronto. They are as follows:

The freight from Toronto to Liverpool on the same machines would be $7.16; only one-half as much as to Regina. To London the charge would be $9.59; to Havre, $8.92; to .Hamburg, $9.75; to Odessa' $12.84; to Buenos Ayres, $12.83; and to Melbourne, $10. So it costs nearly twice as much to deliver a machine in Red Deer as -to deliver the same machine in Melbourne, the most distant part of the earth from Canada. There is one reason why implements are not as cheap as some *would like to see them. Speaking for myself and for my own interests, I would be prepared to say that if we got all our raw materials at an equally reduced duty, either no duty or a duty commensurate with the amount knocked off implements, we could afford, there is no question about that, to reduce the duty on agricultural implements; but it would be at the cost of displacing probably one hundred thousand men in the Dominion of Canada in all these implement works ' and their tributary industries that supply them with raw material. In my judgment, that is too big a price to pay for the small advantage that would be obtained, because, after all, the implements are sold, as I have said, as cheaply as in any country of the earth except the United States and a large part of the difference in that case is
| caused by the larger transportation charges over which we have no control.
As far as I can see, the present financial outlook of Canada is very reassuring. Whether we look at the position of the agriculturist, the workingman, the lumberman, the miner, all the avenues which supply the lifeblood of our trade and commerce appear to me to be thriving and on the up-grade and that in the face of the fact that the reciprocity Bill to which my hon. friend just referred was not accepted. I think that even he, looking at the prosperity of our country and the high prices which the hon. member for Maisonneuve, has given us, will agree that it is well that we did not go into that deal on the occasion when it was offered to us.
I would say in conclusion that a great deal is being said in the papers to-day about the present position of the United States and their tariff and the proposals of President Wilson now before the House. We are told that the United Stated are going in for a kind of free-trade proposition. But that only applies to a very few items, and I give my opinion that when the United States free trade policy under Mr. Wilson is adopted, it will be found that the duties average higher than they do ini the Dominion of Canada to-day without any free trade policy. They have a lohg way to come before they get down to our level. Their -average tariff on dutiable goods is about .forty-five per cent, and vet they are able to manufacture many lines against the world, and do. so. They manufacture in some lines better than a.ny other nation on earth, and, as a matter of fact, they could do with free trade in some lines better than any nation on earth. Yet, with their forty-five per cent tariff they have a long way to come before they get as low as our tariff. Do not let us shout before they get out of the woods over there. Do not let us be too sure that the propositions that President Wilson has put before Congress and the Senate of the United States will be adopted. , He has troubles ahead of him yet. I think it will be found that the propositions that are made there are not going through as easily as is generally supposed. There will be a tremendous upheaval in the United States and trade conditions will be disorganized if they go into effect. Why do I say that ? Wilson represents only about forty per cent of the voters of the United States and the other sixty per cent voted for Taft and Roosevelt, both of whom stood for a higher tariff than that which Wilson has proposed. He has -not at his back nearly half of the people of the United States for his proposition, and if he is a wise man he will go slow.
The cost of living is not going to be materially reduced even if he succeeds in

putting his measure through, but he may succeed in injuring labouring conditions and reducing the workingman's wages. It is a serious proposition. It is easy to say that things ought to be better than they are. We are too ambitious to be content with conditions that are good and I say that the conditions in Canada to-day, whether in regard to the workman or the farmer, are probably as good as they are in any country in the world. Why do I say that ? Because from all nations, from every sea and with every wind that blows, we find immigrants coming into Canada, so that to-day we are speaking about one hundred languages in this Dominion. We offer a home to the people of all the nations of the earth. Why is that ? It is because it is recognized that the conditions in Canada are as good as the best, and there is streaming in from many of the countries of the world, the United States included, a very large influx of people.
That would not obtain unless the conditions in Canada were sound. That is evidence to me that we would be wise in following well beaten paths and not taking up with any fad ideas or any nostrums that may perhaps be put forward as a reason for upsetting conditions as they are. It is a great deal easier to upset conditions that are good than to establish conditions that are better. An examination of the trade statistics and of the speech of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in presenting the budget will convince any man who reads them with a desire to understand things as they are and as they compare with the conditions in any other country in the world, that the conditions that obtain in Canada to-day are unequalled, or at least unexcelled, by those of any other country. That condition has been produced by hard labour, by an immense amount of thought on the part of those who preceded us, by an immense effort on the part of our forefathers who came and hewed out homes for themselves in the province of Ontario under conditions that were perhaps more rugged, more severe, than are exacted from the most distant dwellers in our western or northern country to-day. There are men still living in the province of Ontario who can remember the struggles that were had by tnose who preceded us in the older counties of that province-how wheat and the products of the farm were taken from fifty to seventy-five miles to the point of shipment. The prices that are obtained in the West to-day are very high as compared with the prices that our forefathers obtained in Ontario fifty or seventy-five years ago.
We have seen great changes, we have seen the farmer develop, we have seen him broaden out, until to-day we see him Mr COCKSHUTT.
enjoying a great many of the luxuries of life, driving in his carriage, in some cases in his motor oar, and giving evidence to the world that he is an independent man, a. man who has money and time to enjoy himself and to live in a prosperous way. That is the condition that obtains to-day and if we pursue a wise and sane policy and do not allow ourselves to be carried away with nostrums that may be proposed by those who think that every experiment would be better than a tried doctrine that has stood the test for twenty-five or thirty years and that has proved itself true and good, we will continue to drain from other countries some of the very best blood and a large amount of capital and we will transfer to Canada some of the brawn and muscle to be found in all the enlightened, and it may be some of the unenlightened, nations of the world.
What is the condition to-day in Canada? We are drawing from the United States
150,000	of its citizens per annum most of whom settle in the West as farmers, some coming to Ontario and Quebec to engage in manufacturing industries and bringing their plants and capital with them. We have invested in manufacturing in Canada to-day $300,000,000 of American capital. Only last year the American Steel Company proposed to spend $20,000,000 upon the erection of a steel plant on the shores of the Detroit river. I do not know whether this enterprise will be proceeded with right away but I think it will. Look at the $20,000,000 of American capital invested in and around the city of Hamilton and you will realize from that how much American enterprise has been transplanted to that city. Similarly, we might go through the Dominion of Canada and we find that the conditions that Obtain are tempting men from all the countries of -the world, that we are bringing them in here and affording them conditions which enable them to become prosperous and contented citizens. Whethei you look to the farm, the factory or the mine you will find in Canada enterprise, a reward for labour, a prosperity, a civilization and a Christianity that are equal to those of any country in the world.
Why should we disturb these conditions? Why should we be discontented with conditions that are good and a past that has justified itself? Surely these conditions should not be upset and I trust that we will not have any movement to upset conditions that are sound and true and good and that have given the very best results that the Dominion of Canada has ever experienced.
On motion of Mr. Carvell the debate was adjourned.

On motion of Hon. T. W. White (Minister of Finance), Bill No. 212, respecting certain

sayings banks in the province of Quebec, was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The object of this Bill is to extend for a period of ten years the charters of the Montreal City and District Savings Bank and the Caisse d'Economie de Notre-Dame de Quebec. The capital stock of the City and District Savings Bank is $2,000,000, of which $1,000,000 is paid up; the capital stock of the Caisse d'Economie de Notre-Dame de Quebec is $1,000,000 of which $250,000 is paid up; the total liabilities of the City and District Savings Bank are $30,000,000 and of the Caisse d'Economie $10,000,000; the total assets of the City and District Savings Bank are $32,000,000 and the total assets of the Caisse d'Economie $12,000,000.
Why do these banks not come under the Bank Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have not the same powers as the chartered banks hut their charters expire on the same day. They have no right of note issue nor do they do a discount business. They invest in bonds, debentures, and loan upon collateral security.
Is this Bill based on the Bank Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and that is why I delayed presenting it until it was seen what action this House would take on the Bank Act. The provisions for auditing are very similar.
I suppose this Bill has been very carefully considered?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has. Section 29 is a new clause but it is precisely the same as the clause in the Bank Act. The committee will observe there is a restriction upon the acquisition of real estate to the amount required for the actual use and occupation of the bank.
I suppose they will observe that the same as the bankers observe the Bank Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So far as the clause is concerned the restriction is absolute and I do not think it can be made stronger. By section 34 they are allowed to invest in school bonds or debentures in the Dominion of Canada. Formerly it was confined to the province of Quebec and they requested wide powers and I thought they well might be given them.	"
On section 48-appointment of auditors by shareholders:
t Mr WHITE: I think it is advisable that I should make an explanation with regard to this section. Many members will recall that provision is made in the Bank Act for
external audit, the auditors to be appointed by the shareholders, but from a list selected by ballot by the genera) managers of the chartered banks. These two savings banks do not come under the Bank Act, and are not in any way connected with the Canadian Bankers' Association. Therefore we have not put in any provision that the general managers of the banks shall select the auditors from whom the shareholders shall make the appointments. There is this distinction between two classes of banks: the chartered banks are commercial banks, tanks of discount; these are savings banks and analagous to loan and trust companies in the province of Ontario. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) is acquainted with their mode of operation and audit. The provisions for audit here are practically the same as those appearing in the Bank Act at the time that I presented it to the House, without the qualification of auditors subsequently provided for by the committee. A clause has been inserted here analagous to the clause in the Bank Act:
After the appointment of an auditor or1 auditors under subsection 1 of this section, shareholders the aggregate of whose paid-up capital stock is equal to at least one-third of the paid-up capital stock of the bank, who in writing under their respective hands allege that they are dissatisfied with the appointment so made, may, in and by the same writing, make application to the minister to have the person or persons so appointed superseded, and the minister may, after such inquiry as he may deem necessary, select an auditor or auditors instead of the auditor or auditors appointed at the annual meeting and the auditors so appointed shall thereupon cease to be the auditors of the bank and the auditors so selected shall be the auditors of the bank until the next annual meeting.

Section agreed to.
On section 49-examination by auditor appointed by minister:

I suppose that is in
harmony with section 48.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the same section as appears m the Bank Act, and in substance is to this effect, that the minister may at any time require the auditor appointed by the shareholders, or any other auditor whom he may select, to make inquiry into the affairs or business of the bank. I explained the other day, when the Bank Act was under oonsideraticn that, if the Minister of Finance receives notice of any irregularities, at present he has no .power to make an inquiry, and he is given such power under the provisions of the new Bank Act and under the provisions of this Act.
Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

On motion of Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance) Bill No. 213, respecting the payment of Bounties on Lead contained in lead-bearing ores mined in Canada, was lead the second time, and House went into Committee thereon. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair).
On section 2, sub-section 2-bounties on lead refined in Canada; limitation of amount:
Does this include all that has already been paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. member will look at the preamble he will see that there is unexpended approximately $600,000. Then under this sub-section 2 of section 2, he will see that
The total amount of bounty payable under the provisions of chapter 31 of the statutes of 1903, chapter 13 of the statutes of 1908 (as amended by chapter 37 of the statutes of 1910), and of this Act, shall not exceed two million four hundred and fifty thousand dollars.
That covers all the legislation affecting this matter. My hon. friend was absent when I explained that $2,500,000 was set aside originally, of which about $50,000 was set aside out of that for investigations connected with the zinc industry. Out of the $2,450,000 remaining $1,800,000 was expended on bounties, leaving, as stated, approximately $600,000, which will now be available to pay bounties if required within the period of five years provided by this Bill. The amount to be paid in any one year is not to exceed $250,000. Last year the amount paid was $60,000. At the present prices of lead, no bounty is payable at all.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.
